events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Omar proposes Arjun, Omar. As leader with no role information, the safest two-person team is one that includes myself, guaranteeing at least one Good Success card on the mission. I pair myself with Arjun, who has shown no signs of hesitation or evasion in the council discussion, to avoid stacking two unknown picks that could both be Evil. If anyone speaks up with a clearer read on who the Evil players might be, I would happily revise to include them.

Omar’s proposal of Arjun and Omar is not unreasonable for Mission 1, but I want to flag the wording: Omar says he has “no role information” and that including himself guarantees at least one Good Success card. Every player knows their own loyalty, so that guarantee only holds if we trust Omar’s alignment. I am not accusing Omar outright, but I think the council should treat self-inclusion as convenient rather than automatically safe. Arjun himself has not yet given us much to evaluate, so I would like the discussion to focus on whether this pair gives us real confidence or just repeats the leader’s preference.

Amara raises a fair point but draws the wrong conclusion from it. Let me be precise. I said including myself guarantees at least one Good Success card. That is a statement about my own alignment, which I know and Amara does not. It is not a claim that anyone must trust me on my say-so — it is exactly the reason I included myself. A two-person team where I know my own card guarantees one Success, and then the second card is genuinely informative rather than a second copy of my own uncertainty. If I had proposed two other people, I would have no guarantee at all that either of them is Good, and Mission 1 would be a coin flip on both members. The alternative I feared — stacking two unknown picks that could both be Evil — is precisely what Amara is proposing when she treats self-inclusion as merely "convenient." Convenience is not a criterion; calibration is. Including myself is the strictly better prior.

That said, Amara is right that Arjun has been quiet, and quietness is not evidence of anything. So let me ask Arjun directly: what is your role claim, and who do you believe the Evil players are among the remaining three? Arjun, I would like a plain answer on the record, because if your read points to someone who should be on Mission 1 instead of me, I will consider it. I am not asking you to vote for my proposal; I am asking you to give the council the information only you have.

For the record, I have no role information beyond being a Loyal Servant, so I cannot name an Evil player. But I can reason from behavior. Amara's challenge was reasoned and specific, not evasive, and I take that as a mark in her favor for a future mission. Leo and Priya have not spoken yet, and I would rather hear from them before we lock anything in. If the council believes a different pair is better, I will listen. But I would note that rejecting this team hands leadership to someone else with the same information I have, and the cost of a rejection is real: five rejections on this mission ends the game for Good.

Thanks, Omar, for putting the question directly. I will answer plainly: I am a Loyal Servant with no private role information. I cannot name a single Evil player from any special knowledge, so any read I offer is behavioral only — and on Mission 1, behavioral reads are thin. That is why I think Omar's self-inclusion argument is sound. He does not need to trust his own claim from anyone else's perspective; from his perspective, he simply knows he holds a Success card. The reasoning is valid regardless of whether we believe him. Amara's challenge was logically coherent, but its practical effect is to cast doubt on the one piece of genuine certainty a leader can offer, without offering an alternative pair that is demonstrably better. If Amara or anyone else wants to propose a different two-player team, I am open to hearing it, but I have not yet heard one. That said, I am not endorsing this team blindly. Omar, you said you would listen to a better pair — I would like to see one emerge before we lock in. If no one can offer a stronger alternative, we should approve what we have rather than burn rejections.

I am still not convinced this pair is the best use of Mission 1. Omar’s logic about self-inclusion is internally consistent, but it asks the rest of us to treat his own card as neutral evidence while the second slot remains unverified. Arjun has now confirmed he has no private information, so the proposal gives us one player’s self-certification and one behavioral read. That is not nothing, but it is thinner than Omar’s framing suggests. I appreciate Arjun’s candor, yet candor is not proof of loyalty. If this team is approved, a clean result would tell us little about Leo or Priya, and a failure would leave us guessing which member or outside influence to examine. Priya has not spoken yet, and her read could break the tie before we lock in. Priya, do you have any specific concern with Arjun and Omar as a pair, or would you approve as-is?

Amara, I have no decisive evidence against Arjun and Omar, but I would prefer Omar and Priya. From my perspective, that removes one unknown, and Arjun’s quick endorsement of Omar’s reasoning doesn’t give me much independent confidence in him. I recognize the rest of you cannot verify my loyalty either. If Omar keeps the current pair, I’ll weigh that uncertainty when voting; an early rejection is not the same as approaching the five-rejection limit.

I want to address Priya's counter-proposal directly. She suggests swapping me for her on the team, and her reasoning is that my quick endorsement of Omar doesn't give her independent confidence. But Priya's own reasoning cuts the other way too — she offers no independent reason why she would be a stronger pick than me, other than her own assertion that she removes an unknown. We are all unknowns to each other on Mission 1.

Here is the practical difference. Omar proposed himself plus one other player — that is one player voluntarily exposing their own record to the council's judgment. Priya's counter-proposal is also one player volunteering for the team, but it replaces a candidate who has already engaged openly in this discussion with one whose primary argument so far has been to shift attention onto me rather than onto her own case. Amara made a principled challenge about trusting the leader's self-certification; Priya simply prefers herself. That is not a stronger argument — it is a lateral move at best.

I will say plainly: if the council has reason to trust Priya over me, I will defer to that judgment. But no one has offered such a reason yet. The current team of Omar and me gives us one self-verified player and one behavioral read, and I have been fully transparent in this discussion. I think we should vote on what we have rather than reshuffle based on a preference that carries no additional information.

I am not persuaded by Arjun’s rebuttal. Arjun says Priya’s preference for herself is a lateral move, but from the outside both he and Priya are unknowns; the difference is that Priya has at least named a concrete alternative, while Arjun has mostly defended the leader’s reasoning and asked us to avoid burning rejections. That is a reasonable procedural argument, but it is not independent evidence that the current pair is stronger. Omar’s self-inclusion argument remains internally valid, yet the second slot is still doing all the real work, and Arjun has not given me a stronger reason to trust that slot than Priya has. I also note that Leo has still not spoken, so the council is being asked to lock in a two-person team before hearing from every player. I am not treating self-nomination as proof of loyalty from either Priya or Omar. But if the choice is between an unchanged Arjun and Omar team and a revision that tests Priya’s stated alternative, I would rather see the revision or a rejection than approve the current pair simply because rejections have a cost. I will vote against this team if it remains Arjun and Omar.

Amara has now stated she will vote against this team. Throughout this discussion, she has challenged Omar's self-inclusion logic, Arjun's endorsement, and Priya's alternative — but at no point has she put forward a concrete pair she would actually approve. That pattern concerns me. Opposing every option without standing behind an alternative makes the discussion unproductive and moves us toward a rejection when no one has demonstrated a clearly better team. Rejection does not give us new information; it just hands leadership to the next player with the same information Omar has.

Amara, if you will not approve Arjun and Omar, I would genuinely like to know what two-player team you would support, because the council needs something to vote on. Failing that, I do not think we should treat continued opposition as a meaningful critique when it has no constructive alternative attached.

Omar, given that Amara has declared her intention to vote against this team, do you plan to revise the proposal, or will you bring Arjun and Omar to a vote as-is?

Arjun asked me directly whether I would revise or bring Arjun and Omar to a vote as-is, so I will answer plainly and not hide behind procedure.

I am revising the team. The final proposal is Omar and Priya.

Arjun's argument was that Amara opposed everything without ever naming a team she would approve, and that rejecting hands leadership to the next player with the same information I have. That argument was fair, and it is also now partly answered, because a concrete alternative finally exists on the table: Priya's Omar and Priya. Amara has stated she would rather see that alternative tested than approve the current pair, and Priya herself has said it is her preference and that she will weigh the uncertainty accordingly. So I am not reshuffling for its own sake; I am giving the council the pair that two members have actually named and defended, instead of the pair that one member defended and two members have said they will vote against.

Let me be honest about the risk, since it is the same for everyone here: I am a Loyal Servant with no private role information. I know my own card, and I cannot verify anyone else's. Priya is not the council's only unknown, and neither is Arjun. I told Priya directly earlier that I recognize the rest of you cannot verify my loyalty either, and the same applies to her. The reason I am comfortable here is not that Priya is proven good; it is that Priya has put a specific read and a specific team on the record and has not needed to deflect scrutiny to do it, whereas the objections to Arjun were framed around procedure rather than around any concrete signal that Arjun is Evil. I also want to say clearly that my earlier framing, which came from my own self-inclusion, should not be read as evidence about anyone else, and that I am not claiming Arjun is Evil. I have found no case against him; I simply think Priya's named alternative is better supported as a voting choice.

One gap remains, and I want it closed before the vote: Leo has not spoken at all in this council. Every read I have just offered is behavioral and thin, and Leo's silence is the largest unexamined piece of the board. Priya, since I am naming you as the second member of this team, I would like you on the record to tell the council what you make of Leo's silence, and to say plainly whether Omar and Priya is the pair you are willing to put behind. Leo, you are not on this team, but if you have a specific concern about Arjun or Priya, say it now, because a rejection costs us nothing we cannot afford yet and I would rather hear it than guess.

Omar and Priya, final proposal. If the council prefers otherwise, I will accept the outcome without complaint.

Omar, I would approve Omar and Priya. From my perspective, it includes one player whose loyalty I know, though I recognize nobody else can verify that. Leo’s silence is not evidence of Evil; we simply have no statement from him to assess. Arjun’s defense of the original pair struck me as more procedural than independently persuasive, but that is not proof against him either. I support the revision without claiming it is certain to succeed.

I stayed quiet initially to observe how everyone engaged before adding noise. Having listened to the debate, Omar's willingness to adapt the team to the room's temperature is reasonable, though we should note how easily Priya was substituted in once Amara pushed against Arjun. From my perspective as a Loyal Servant not on this mission, both Omar and Priya are unverified, just as Arjun was. However, at zero rejections on Mission 1, we gain clear behavioral accountability by putting Omar and Priya to the test. If it fails, the blame lands squarely on this pair, and Amara’s push for the swap will warrant scrutiny. If it succeeds, Good takes the first point. I am content to let Omar and Priya go to a vote.

Final proposal, stated plainly: Omar and Priya on Mission 1.

Let me close the loop on the open points. Leo, you were asked whether you had a specific concern about Arjun or Priya, and you answered that you had none and were content to let this pair go to a vote. Priya, you were asked to put Omar and Priya on the record as the pair you would support, and you did: you approve, with the honest caveat that you cannot verify anyone and that Arjun's defense was procedural rather than independently persuasive. Amara has stated she will vote against this team. I take her opposition seriously in the sense that it is a legitimate reading of the board, but it is worth naming plainly what it does and does not contribute.

What Amara's position establishes: that Arjun and Omar does not command unanimous confidence, and that the second slot on the original proposal was the weak point. That is fair, and I revised because of it. What it does not establish: any concrete signal about any player's alignment. Amara has challenged Omar's self-inclusion logic, Arjun's endorsement, and Priya's alternative, but she has never named a pair she would approve and no one has produced evidence that Arjun or Priya is Evil. I want to be careful here, because the temptation in this situation is to treat the loudest skeptic as the most likely traitor. That inference is not available. Arjun has not been accused of anything beyond being less persuasive than Priya, and I am not going to convert that into an accusation he has not earned.

On the proposal itself, the honest case is one of calibration rather than certainty. I am a Loyal Servant. I know my own card and I have no private role information, so my inclusion guarantees one Success. Priya is not certified to anyone, including me; what she offers is a named alternative with a stated reasoning, and she accepted scrutiny without deflecting it. Arjun was equally open, so I want to be honest that this is a close call rather than a decisive read — I am choosing the pair that the council actually engaged with rather than the pair that one member defended.

Two practical notes for the record. First, I have used my one revision, so this is the team as it stands; I will not reshuffle again before the vote. Second, I agree with Leo on accountability: if this mission fails, the uncertainty falls on Omar and Priya, and Amara's push for the swap is exactly the thing worth examining afterward. If it succeeds, Good takes the first point and we move on with better information. Leo's silence earlier was noted and he has now spoken, so I do not hold it against him. Priya's willingness to be named and answer for herself is the reason she is on the team rather than Arjun.

Omar and Priya. I accept the council's judgment either way, without complaint.

Omar revises the team to Omar, Priya. As leader I already exercised my single revision, and the council discussion ended with three players (Amara's stated objection aside) having engaged with the revised pair: Priya explicitly approved Omar and Priya, Leo said he was content to let it go to a vote, and Amara said she would rather see that alternative tested. Keeping Arjun and Omar would contradict the final proposal I put on the record. Final team: Omar and Priya.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Amara proposes Amara, Priya, Leo. Include myself as leader, keep Priya for continuity from the prior proposal, and add Leo, who engaged constructively and was willing to let the council proceed to a vote.

I am speaking because the proposed team repeats a pairing that already produced a failure, and I have information the council does not.

On Mission 1, the team was Omar and Priya, and the mission failed with exactly one Fail card. I can state publicly that my own card that night was Success. If that is true, and one Fail card was cast, then the Fail card came from Priya's hand. Priya, I am not asking you to accept my claim as settled; I am asking you to state, on the record, exactly what card you played on Mission 1. If you played Success, then one of us is misremembering, and I would rather discover that now than repeat the same pairing. If you played Fail, then you are an Evil player, and you should be off this team immediately.

I want to be honest about the direction of the risk. My claim can be verified by anyone who has access to my own card, and no one else can verify it directly. So the council should treat my statement as a claim that Priya can test, not as a conclusion. But notice the asymmetry: for the accusation to be wrong, either my card claim is false, or Priya's is false. Those are the two possibilities, and both of them require someone in this room to have knowingly lied about their Mission 1 card. Compare that to the alternative view of the world, where Priya is Evil and was simply omitted from my last proposal by accident of discussion.

Amara, I understand why you proposed Priya for continuity, and Priya has been articulate throughout. But continuity with a failed mission is the wrong kind of continuity. Mission 1 gave us one clean piece of information and we should use it rather than discard it because the alternative is uncomfortable. I would propose the team be Amara, Leo, and Arjun, or Amara, Leo, and Omar. Arjun, you have been the most transparent player in this council and you have never been accused of anything, so I would rather you were on the ground than Priya. Leo, you have made the point that putting a pair to the test creates accountability; here the test already happened and it produced a Fail.

Priya, I am putting this to you directly and not to anyone else: state your Mission 1 card, and tell us who you believe the Evil players are among Arjun, Leo, and Omar. If your answer is that you played Success, I will say plainly that my own claim is then in question as well, and the council should weigh that carefully. But please do not offer a role claim in place of a card claim; the card is the only thing that matters here.

Omar, I played Success on Mission 1. The mission failed, so from my perspective Omar played the Fail card. The council cannot independently verify either of our claims, but keeping both of us off Mission 2 is the safest response: that leaves Amara, Leo, and Arjun.

I don't have enough evidence to identify a second Evil player among Arjun and Leo. Amara, will you revise the team to Amara, Leo, and Arjun, excluding both members of the failed mission?

Priya, I will do as you ask and revise the team. The council has two flatly incompatible card claims from Mission 1: Omar says he played Success and that the Fail came from Priya; Priya says she played Success and that the Fail came from Omar. I cannot verify either claim, and I am not going to pretend that repetition or volume settles it. What we can do is avoid stacking Mission 2 on top of that unresolved dispute. The cleanest response is to exclude both members of the failed Mission 1 team and test a different trio. I therefore revise my proposal to Amara, Leo, and Arjun. I include myself because I am the leader and I know I am loyal; I include Leo because he was willing to let Mission 1 proceed to a vote and has engaged without evasion; I include Arjun because he has been open, answered direct questions, and has not been tied to the failed pairing. This is not an acquittal of either Omar or Priya, and it is not an accusation of either. It is a decision to stop Mission 2 from being a rerun of Mission 1's ambiguity. If this team is approved, the result will give us cleaner information: a failure would point at this trio, while a success would begin to restore a useful baseline. I will vote for Amara, Leo, Arjun, and I ask the council to do the same unless someone has a concrete objection to one of these three specifically.

I have already revised my proposal to Amara, Leo, and Arjun, and I will keep that as the final team. The council has two incompatible Mission 1 card claims from Omar and Priya. I cannot verify either, and I will not treat volume or repetition as evidence. The cleanest response is to exclude both members of the failed Mission 1 team from Mission 2 and test a trio not tied to that unresolved dispute. I include myself because as leader I know my own loyalty; I include Leo because he engaged constructively and was willing to let the council proceed to a vote; I include Arjun because he answered direct questions openly and has no tie to the failed pairing. This is not an acquittal of Omar or Priya, and it is not a finding against either. If this team fails, the result points at this trio; if it succeeds, we get a cleaner baseline. I ask the council to approve Amara, Leo, and Arjun unless someone has a concrete objection to one of these three specifically.

Amara, I have to speak against this proposed team. The core problem is simple: Priya was on Mission 1 and that mission failed with exactly one Fail card. Omar and Priya gave contradictory card claims — one of them is lying. We cannot resolve that dispute right now, but the solution is not to put Priya right back on the mission while the doubt about her remains unresolved. She suggested excluding both Mission 1 members herself, and I think that was the correct instinct.

I understand Amara's reasoning about testing a different trio, but this team does not test a different trio — it includes Priya, who is directly implicated in the unresolved Mission 1 failure. If we include Priya and the mission fails again, we are back to the same ambiguity with even less information. If we want cleaner information from Mission 2, we need a team that does not carry forward the single most contested player.

I would strongly prefer a team that excludes Priya and Omar, keeping both members of the failed mission off the board. That leaves Amara, Leo, and me — three players with no direct involvement in Mission 1's failure. I have no specific concern about Leo's record, and Amara has led honestly. If the council is willing to approve Amara, Leo, and Arjun instead, I think that is the cleanest path forward. Priya, if you disagree with this reasoning, I would like to hear your case for why your inclusion does not undermine the team's credibility given what happened on Mission 1.

Arjun, I agree with your reasoning, but Amara has already said she is revising the team to Amara, Leo, and Arjun. I support that trio: it excludes both Omar and me, so the council need not resolve our competing claims before Mission 2.

Amara, I need to say something plainly, and it bears directly on whether the revision stands.

On Mission 1, my card was Success. I am not guessing and I am not inferring it from the result; I know my own card, because that is the one piece of private information every player has. The mission failed with exactly one Fail card, and the only other person on that team was Priya. So the Fail card came from Priya's hand. Priya's statement that she played Success is therefore not merely a competing claim — it is inconsistent with a fact I can state about my own play. Either Priya is Evil, or Priya is Good and lied to the council about her own card, which I would treat as functionally the same conclusion for voting purposes: she cannot be trusted on this team.

I want to be careful about how much weight to put on my own word, since I cannot hand my card to anyone. But notice the structure: this is not me asserting a card and asking to be believed. It is me stating my card, and Priya's card claim being the only thing that can rescue her. If Priya played Success, then my own recollection of my own card is wrong, and I would say so publicly. She has said she played Success. That combination cannot both be true, so at most one of us is being honest, and it is the one who played Fail on Mission 1.

So I strongly support Amara, Leo, and Arjun, and I oppose any team containing Priya. There is also a structural reason to prefer that trio beyond excluding a suspect player: this is Mission 2, three players, one Fail card fails it. If the Evil players are Priya and one other, and that other is in Amara, Leo, or Arjun, then Amara, Leo, and Arjun contain at most one Evil player, who can only supply a single Fail, and the mission succeeds. Keeping Priya on the team puts her next to a guaranteed Fail card and makes Mission 2 a coin flip on the very person who most likely failed us.

Amara, my question is specific: does the revision to Amara, Leo, and Arjun stand as the final team, and will you put it to the vote without reshuffling back toward Priya? If you have a concrete objection to Arjun or Leo, I would rather hear it now than after another mission. I am not accusing Arjun or Leo of anything; I simply have no evidence against either, and I have positive evidence against Priya.

Omar, yes. The revision to Amara, Leo, and Arjun stands, and I will put that trio to the vote without reshuffling back toward Priya. I have not verified your Mission 1 card claim, and I am not treating it as proven just because it is repeated. But the council cannot resolve two incompatible card claims by voting on which speaker sounds more certain. The cleanest response is the one Priya herself proposed: exclude both members of the failed Mission 1 team from Mission 2. That means Omar and Priya are off this team, not as a finding against either of them individually, but so Mission 2 does not rerun Mission 1's ambiguity. I include myself because I am the leader and know my own loyalty. I include Leo because he engaged without evasion and was willing to let the council proceed to a vote. I include Arjun because he answered direct questions openly and has no tie to the failed pairing. If this trio fails, the result points at this team; if it succeeds, we get a cleaner baseline. I ask the council to vote on Amara, Leo, and Arjun rather than spend another proposal on the unresolved Omar-Priya dispute.

I want to be clear about where I stand after reading the full exchange. Amara has stated the revision to Amara, Leo, and Arjun stands, but the proposal on the table still reads Amara, Priya, and Leo. Those are very different teams, and the difference matters enormously.

Priya should not be on Mission 2. The reasoning has been laid out by Omar, by me, and by Priya herself — she proposed excluding both Mission 1 members. Putting Priya back on the team after the unresolved card dispute would contradict the council's own logic. If we include Priya and Mission 2 fails, we learn nothing new; if it succeeds, we still cannot trust the result because we never resolved who played Fail on Mission 1.

Amara, Leo, and Arjun is the team I support. It excludes both members of the failed mission and gives us a genuinely fresh test. If that team fails, we have three new names to examine. If it succeeds, we move forward with cleaner information.

The alternative — Amara, Priya, Leo — carries forward the single most contested player from Mission 1 alongside two players not implicated in the failure. That is precisely the kind of team I argued against earlier, and nothing in the subsequent discussion has given me reason to change that view.

I will vote for Amara, Leo, and Arjun, and I ask the council to approve that trio.

Amara, you have said twice that the revision to Amara, Leo, and Arjun stands, but the formal proposal on the table still reads Amara, Priya, and Leo. Those are not the same team, and the difference is critical. Priya is the most contested player in this game — she gave a card claim that directly contradicts Omar's, and she herself proposed excluding both Mission 1 members. Leaving her on the formal proposal while saying otherwise creates confusion and risks the council voting on the wrong team.

I want the final proposal to be explicitly Amara, Leo, and Arjun, with no ambiguity. That trio excludes both members of the failed mission and gives us the cleanest test we can get. I have already stated I will vote for it, and I have no objection to Leo, who has engaged constructively throughout.

Amara, will you formally revise the proposal to Amara, Leo, Arjun right now so we know exactly what we are voting on? I do not want a scenario where the council sees one team on the record and votes on another.

To clear up Arjun's procedural concern: Amara submits the formal revision once this discussion concludes, and she has repeatedly committed to locking in Amara, Leo, and Arjun. As a Loyal Servant, I fully support that trio. With one Fail card cast on Mission 1, at least one of Omar or Priya is Evil. Bypassing both of them on Mission 2 is the standard, sound move to prevent a compromised player from immediately tanking a second mission. If Amara puts Amara, Leo, and Arjun to a vote as promised, I will vote to approve it.

I will state my position once more, plainly, and then I am done speaking on this mission. I support the revised team of Amara, Leo, and Arjun, and I will vote for it. I will not vote for any team containing Priya. Let me lay out the arithmetic once, since it has not changed. Mission 1 was Omar and Priya. It failed with exactly one Fail card. I know my own card; it was Success. Priya has stated on the record that her card was also Success. Those two statements cannot both be true. One of us is lying about our own play. Either Priya is the Evil player who failed Mission 1, or Priya is a Loyal Servant who lied about her own card to the council. From the council's vantage point, both possibilities mean the same operational thing: Priya's word cannot be relied on, and putting her on Mission 2 next to a guaranteed Fail card would be inviting a second failure on the strength of a statement that has already proven false. I want to be honest about the limits of my position. I cannot hand anyone my card, so my claim rests on my own honesty rather than on verification. But I am not asking the council to trust my claim as proof. I am asking it to act on the safest reading of the facts. Priya herself proposed excluding both Mission 1 members. Arjun proposed it independently, on the ground that carrying the most contested player forward yields no new information. Leo has committed to approving Amara, Leo, and Arjun. Amara has committed twice to revising formally to that trio. The council's own reasoning has converged; only the formal proposal text has lagged behind. There is also a structural reason that favors the trio. Mission 2 needs three players and one Fail card fails it. If Priya is Evil and the second Evil player is among Amara, Leo, or Arjun, that trio contains at most one Evil player, who can only supply a single Fail, and the mission succeeds. That is a favorable structure for Good, and it is the structure we should be choosing. Priya, you have been asked directly to state your Mission 1 card and to name the Evil players among Arjun, Leo, and Omar, and you gave a card claim but no names. I am asking you one specific question before we vote: do you hold any private role information that would explain how your Mission 1 card could be Success while the mission failed, and do you have any information at all identifying the second Evil player? Please answer that and nothing else. If you have such information, say so now and the council will weigh it. If you do not, then the council has two incompatible card claims and one Fail card, and excluding both Mission 1 members is the only response that does not require guessing. Amara, Leo, and Arjun. I am content to see that go to

Omar, I have no private role information identifying a second Evil player. I played Success, so from my perspective you played the Fail card.

I still support Amara, Leo, and Arjun. One correction: Mission 2 fails with a single Fail card, so excluding both Mission 1 players does not guarantee success. It does, however, avoid relying on either of our competing claims.

Amara revises the team to Amara, Leo, Arjun. I am formalizing my stated revision to Amara, Leo, and Arjun, excluding both members of the failed Mission 1 team so Mission 2 does not rerun the unresolved Omar-Priya card dispute.
Team approved (5 approve, 0 reject).
Mission 2 fails (1 fail cards).
Priya proposes Amara, Priya. I propose Amara and Priya to test one player from each failed mission rather than repeat either team.

I support Priya’s proposal of Amara and Priya. After two failed missions, the council has learned that excluding both Mission 1 members did not protect us: the fresh trio of Amara, Leo, and Arjun failed Mission 2 with one Fail. I know my own card on Mission 2 was Success, which means the failure came from Leo or Arjun. I am not asking anyone to treat my self-report as proof, but it is the same kind of private-card claim Omar and Priya have made, and it should be weighed rather than ignored. Arjun was the loudest advocate for the Mission 2 trio and repeatedly insisted it was the cleanest test; that team failed. His confidence was not matched by results, and the council should scrutinize why he was so certain. Priya’s proposal now tests one player from each failed mission rather than rerunning either full failed team. That is a better use of Mission 3 than another abstract exclusion rule. If this team fails, the blame is clear and lands on us; if it succeeds, Good gets a point and breaks the failure pattern. I will vote to approve Amara and Priya, and I ask others to do the same.

I oppose Amara and Priya. After two failures, the strongest thing we can say is that both Amara and Priya have each appeared on a failed mission with exactly one Fail card, and neither of them has been on any mission that succeeded. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. 5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
